title: Is polar day half the year?
hook: At the North Pole the Sun rises once a year. How long does it stay up?

knows: that the poles get months of daylight and months of darkness
that the Sun is at the pole between the equinoxes
doesNotKnow: that the sunlit half and the dark half of the polar year are unequal

misconception: The Sun is up at the North Pole for exactly half the year, six months of 182.6 days.
objective: The learner can say that at the North Pole the Sun is up about 186 days and down about 179, because Earth moves slower in northern summer.

claims.text: On this stage's model the Sun is above the pole's horizon for 186 days (March equinox to September equinox) and below for 179.
claims.source: Builder's node check of the Kepler model (e = 0.016709, perihelion longitude 283 deg, year 365.2564 d, obliquity 23.44 deg): equinox-to-equinox 186.41 d and 178.84 d, pole in daylight while declination > 0 (geometric, no refraction). The stage and reveal use the same code (solar model in Demo.tsx). Equation of time and precession ignored; the 283 deg value is from memory.

claims.text: The summer half is 7.6 days longer than the winter half.
claims.source: 186.41 - 178.84 = 7.57 d (c1). The brief's published check: March-to-September equinox intervals are about 186 days (USNO 'Earth's Seasons'; from memory, needs a checker).

claims.text: Earth is farthest from the Sun in early July and moves slowest there, so the half of the orbit from the March equinox to the September equinox takes longer.
claims.source: Kepler's second law; aphelion in early July is from memory (about 4-5 July). The model's perihelion longitude 283 deg puts perihelion in early January.

claims.text: Counting light bent by air and the Sun's width, the polar day is about 190 days.
claims.source: From the brief (cm-geography): counting sunrise at the upper limb with refraction gives 190.7 days (its Kepler script). Not independently checked by the builder.

claims.text: At the North Pole the Sun rises once a year and sets once a year.
claims.source: Sun's declination is positive once per year; stage shows one rise at the March equinox and one set at the September equinox. Exact only for the geometric model.

claims.text: Stage: North Pole seen from above, shaded half is night, the Sun's noon direction is fixed at longitude 0; the corner shows Earth's orbit drawn far more oval (eccentricity 0.4, not the real 0.017) so the two halves are visible, with the days in each half.
claims.source: Model label on the stage; the longitude is arbitrary and the daily spin is ignored. Night = circle of 90 degrees around the antisolar point.

recall.question: At the North Pole, is the Sun up for exactly half the year?
options: No, a few days more than half
No, a few days less than half
recall.why: Earth is slower in northern summer, so the Sun stays above the pole's horizon about 186 days and below about 179.
